On this page

Asynchronous Runtimes by Target ​

This page sets guidance for contributors working on Feluqa's runtime architecture. It is not a rule that every Application must use the same executor.

Async syntax is not a runtime ​

Rust's async functions and blocks produce values that implement Future. Calling an async function creates a future; it does not, by itself, run that future. An executor polls futures and wakes them when the work they await can continue. A runtime commonly adds target-specific services such as timers and network I/O. See the Rust async book for the language and executor model.

We keep these concepts separate in Feluqa's APIs because shared business logic should not depend on a particular executor. Runtime-specific facilities belong to the target profile that provides them.

Server profile: Tokio ​

The current Feluqa server profile uses Tokio for networking, timers, and task execution. We keep Tokio as an external dependency because its established runtime and ecosystem meet the server profile's current needs. Reimplementing it or maintaining a fork would duplicate upstream's compatibility, security, and maintenance work. We would revisit this choice only if a verified requirement could not be met upstream.

We keep Tokio dependencies and types within the server profile so feluqa-core, portable contracts, and no_std surfaces do not inherit a server runtime. Shared APIs avoid Tokio-specific handles and synchronization types because those would tie other target profiles to the server executor.

We treat vendoring as a build and supply-chain decision, for example for an audited offline build. It does not require taking ownership of a runtime fork.

Embedded and real-time targets ​

no_std does not choose an executor. We select the executor, timers, hardware abstraction layer, and allocation policy based on each target's actual requirements.

OptionRoleEvaluation notes
EmbassyAsync embedded ecosystem with executors, time support, networking components, and selected hardware abstraction layers.We consider Embassy when an embedded Application benefits from its cooperative async model and supported hardware. Task allocation depends on executor configuration and features, so we do not describe all tasks as statically allocated by default.
RTIC 2Interrupt-driven concurrency framework with priorities and resource scheduling; v2 software tasks use async functions.We consider RTIC when an Application's interrupt and priority model fits. Hard real-time guarantees still require a defined timing model and analysis of the complete system.
futures-utilUtilities and combinators for working with futures, rather than a complete executor/runtime.For constrained libraries, we disable default features and select only the utilities needed. Each utility has its own feature and allocation requirements; alloc enables heap-dependent functionality, and omitting it does not make every utility available.

Embassy and RTIC solve different scheduling and hardware problems. They are options to evaluate per target, not interchangeable defaults for every Feluqa profile. Embassy documents its executor configuration and allocation modes in the Embassy Book.

Selection checklist ​

We evaluate a runtime dependency against:

  • the target profile and hardware or operating system;
  • whether std, alloc, or neither is available;
  • required networking, timers, hardware drivers, and executor facilities;
  • concurrency and latency goals, including any hard deadlines;
  • measured flash, RAM, stack, and scheduling costs on the target;
  • dependency license, maintenance, MSRV, target support, and unsafe surface.

We do not describe an async runtime as providing hard real-time guarantees by itself because timing depends on the complete system. We keep server runtime dependencies out of portable and embedded contracts because shared application-level async functions do not require a shared executor.
